title: Νέστορος διήγησις
titleEn: The Cattle-Raid and the Charge — Iliad 11.655–803
about: Nestor answers Patroclus with a long speech. He asks why Achilles should grieve for the wounded Achaeans and yet do nothing for them, and wishes himself young again, as he was in the war between the Pylians and the Epeans of Elis. He tells how he killed Itymoneus in a cattle-raid, how the Pylians shared the spoil and the debts owed them, how the Epeans came against Thryoessa, and how, kept from the fight by his father Neleus, he still stood out among the horsemen, killed Mulius and took fifty chariots, and was stopped from killing the Molions only because Poseidon hid them in mist. Then he turns to Patroclus and recalls the day he and Odysseus came to the house of Peleus to gather men for Troy, and the charges that Peleus gave Achilles and Menoetius gave Patroclus. He asks Patroclus to speak to Achilles, and if Achilles will not fight, to lead the Myrmidons out in Achilles’ armour so that the Trojans, taking him for Achilles, will give the Achaeans time to breathe.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα Γερήνιος ἱππότα Νέστωρ·
sentences.l: Him then answered the Gerenian horseman Nestor:
sentences.i: Then the Gerenian horseman Nestor answered him:
sentences.n: This is the whole-line reply formula, and Nestor’s speech follows in the next unit. ἠμείβετ’ is the imperfect of ἀμείβομαι ‘answer’ with its final vowel elided; Γερήνιος ‘Gerenian’ is Nestor’s stock epithet, of uncertain origin, and ἱππότα is the epic nominative of ἱππότης ‘horseman’. The paragraph opens here, and Nestor is answering the speech of Patroclus that closed the last part.

sentences.t:
τίπτε τὰρ ὧδ’ Ἀχιλεὺς ὀλοφύρεται υἷας Ἀχαιῶν,
ὅσσοι δὴ βέλεσιν βεβλήαται;
sentences.l:
“Why ever, then, does Achilles so grieve for the sons of the Achaeans,
all who have indeed been struck by missiles?
sentences.i: “Why does Achilles grieve like this for the sons of the Achaeans, all who have been struck by missiles?
sentences.n: Nestor answers Patroclus by asking why Achilles should pity the Achaeans at all. τίπτε is τί ποτε ‘why ever’; τὰρ is probably τοι ἄρ run together and adds a note of impatience. ὀλοφύρεται ‘grieves for’ takes υἷας, the epic accusative plural of υἱός ‘son’. βεβλήαται is the perfect passive of βάλλω ‘strike’, with Ionic -αται for -νται, and βέλεσιν is the dative plural of βέλος ‘missile’.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τι οἶδε
πένθεος, ὅσσον ὄρωρε κατὰ στρατόν·
sentences.l:
And he knows nothing at all
of the grief, how great has arisen throughout the army;
sentences.i: And he knows nothing at all of the grief, how great it has grown throughout the army;
sentences.n: οὐδέ τι οἶδε ‘and he knows nothing at all’ still belongs to the question, with Achilles as its subject. πένθεος is the genitive of πένθος ‘grief’ in its open epic form (Attic πένθους). ὅσσον ὄρωρε is ‘how great … has arisen’, ὄρωρε being the perfect of ὄρνυμι in its intransitive sense, and κατὰ στρατόν is ‘throughout the army’.

sentences.t:
οἳ γὰρ ἄριστοι
ἐν νηυσὶν κέαται βεβλημένοι οὐτάμενοί τε.
sentences.l:
for those who are the best
lie in the ships, struck and wounded.
sentences.i: for the best of the men lie in the ships, struck and wounded.
sentences.n: οἳ γὰρ ἄριστοι ‘for those who are the best’ gives the reason for the grief. κέαται is the epic third plural of κεῖμαι ‘lie’ (Attic κεῖνται). The two participles say how: βεβλημένοι ‘struck’ is from βάλλω, a blow from a missile, and οὐτάμενοι ‘wounded’ is from οὐτάω, the verb the next lines pair with it again.

sentences.t:
βέβληται μὲν ὃ Τυδεΐδης κρατερὸς Διομήδης,
οὔτασται δ’ Ὀδυσεὺς δουρὶ κλυτὸς ἠδ’ Ἀγαμέμνων·
sentences.l:
Struck is he, the Tydeus’-son, strong Diomedes,
and wounded is Odysseus, famous with the spear, and Agamemnon;
sentences.i: The son of Tydeus, strong Diomedes, has been struck, and Odysseus, famous with the spear, is wounded, and Agamemnon too;
sentences.n: Nestor names the wounded leaders. ὃ is the pronoun ‘he’ (the Homeric article), with Τυδεΐδης in apposition, the patronymic ‘son of Tydeus’, and κρατερός ‘strong’ is Diomedes’ stock epithet. βέβληται and οὔτασται are perfect passives, ‘has been struck’ and ‘has been wounded’. δουρὶ κλυτός ‘famous with the spear’ is an epithet used of several fighters, here of Odysseus; ἠδ’ ‘and’ adds Agamemnon.

sentences.t: βέβληται δὲ καὶ Εὐρύπυλος κατὰ μηρὸν ὀϊστῷ·
sentences.l: and struck also is Eurypylus in the thigh by an arrow;
sentences.i: and Eurypylus too has been struck in the thigh by an arrow;
sentences.n: Eurypylus, whose wound the last part describes, is added to the list. κατὰ μηρόν is ‘in the thigh’, with the accusative of the part hit, and ὀϊστῷ is the dative of ὀϊστός ‘arrow’, the means; the edition prints the diaeresis. The verb is βέβληται again, as at 660.

sentences.t:
τοῦτον δ’ ἄλλον ἐγὼ νέον ἤγαγον ἐκ πολέμοιο
ἰῷ ἀπὸ νευρῆς βεβλημένον.
sentences.l:
and this other man I myself lately brought out of the war,
struck by an arrow from the bowstring.
sentences.i: And this other man, struck by an arrow from the bowstring, I have just brought out of the fighting myself.
sentences.n: τοῦτον … ἄλλον is ‘this other one’; Nestor means Machaon, the wounded man whose carrying off the previous part describes, but does not name him. νέον is the adverb ‘lately, just now’, and ἤγαγον is the aorist of ἄγω ‘bring’. ἰῷ is the dative of ἰός ‘arrow’, and ἀπὸ νευρῆς ‘from the bowstring’ says where the shot came from; βεβλημένον agrees with τοῦτον.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ἀχιλλεὺς
ἐσθλὸς ἐὼν Δαναῶν οὐ κήδεται οὐδ’ ἐλεαίρει.
sentences.l:
But Achilles,
good though he is, does not care for the Danaans, nor pity them.
sentences.i: But Achilles, good man though he is, has no care for the Danaans and no pity.
sentences.n: ἐσθλὸς ἐών is ‘good though he is’, the participle taken as concessive, and ‘good’ is the usual translation of ἐσθλός, here said bitterly. κήδεται and ἐλεαίρει are ‘cares for’ and ‘pities’, a pair that also stands together at 2.27, with Δαναῶν ‘of the Danaans’ as the object of both. Nestor uses Danaans here, Achaeans before, and Argives two lines on.

sentences.l:
Does he wait until the swift ships near the sea,
against the will of the Argives, are warmed by hostile fire,
and we ourselves are killed in a row?
sentences.i: Is he waiting until the swift ships by the sea are set burning by hostile fire, against the will of the Argives, and we ourselves are killed one after another?
sentences.n: ἦ opens a question. μένει εἰς ὅ κε … θέρωνται is ‘waits until … are warmed’: θέρωνται, the subjunctive of θέρομαι ‘warm oneself’, is a grim understatement for ships catching fire, and the English says ‘set burning’. ἀέκητι with the genitive is ‘against the will of’, πυρὸς δηΐοιο is ‘hostile fire’, and ἐπισχερώ is ‘in a row, one after another’. The question ends at the Greek question mark.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ἐμὴ ἲς
ἔσθ’ οἵη πάρος ἔσκεν ἐνὶ γναμπτοῖσι μέλεσσιν.
sentences.l:
For my force is not
such as formerly it was in my pliant limbs.
sentences.i: for my strength is not what it used to be in my supple limbs.
sentences.n: This gives the reason (γάρ) why Nestor cannot act himself: old age has taken his strength. οὐ … ἔσθ’ οἵη πάρος ἔσκεν is ‘is not such as it was before’; ἔσκεν is the iterative past of εἰμί (the suffix -σκ-), ‘used to be’. ἲς is ‘force, strength’, and γναμπτοῖσι μέλεσσιν is ‘in pliant limbs’, γναμπτός meaning ‘bent, supple’ and μέλεσσιν being the epic dative plural of μέλος ‘limb’.

sentences.t:
εἴθ’ ὣς ἡβώοιμι βίη δέ μοι ἔμπεδος εἴη
ὡς ὁπότ’ Ἠλείοισι καὶ ἡμῖν νεῖκος ἐτύχθη
ἀμφὶ βοηλασίῃ,
sentences.l:
If only I were so young, and my strength were firm,
as when between the Eleans and us a quarrel arose
about cattle-driving,
sentences.i: If only I were as young as that, and my strength were firm, as it was when a quarrel arose between us and the Eleans over a cattle-raid,
sentences.n: Nestor wishes himself young again, in the same first line as at 7.157. εἴθ’ with the optative ἡβώοιμι (ἡβάω ‘be in one’s prime’, with the open epic ending) states a wish that cannot be fulfilled; ὡς ὁπότ’ ‘as when’ points to the time of the cattle-raid. ἐτύχθη is the passive aorist of τεύχω ‘make’, so ‘a quarrel was made’, i.e. broke out. βοηλασίῃ, from βοῦς ‘ox’ and ἐλαύνω ‘drive’, is cattle-driving. The same people are Eleans here and Epeans from 688.

sentences.t:
ὅτ’ ἐγὼ κτάνον Ἰτυμονῆα
ἐσθλὸν Ὑπειροχίδην, ὃς ἐν Ἤλιδι ναιετάασκε,
ῥύσι’ ἐλαυνόμενος·
sentences.i: when I killed Itymoneus, the good son of Hypeirochus, who lived in Elis, as I was driving off goods in reprisal;
sentences.n: The time-clause goes on with ὅτ’ ‘when’ and names the man Nestor killed. Ὑπειροχίδην is the patronymic ‘son of Hypeirochus’, in the accusative with Ἰτυμονῆα, and ναιετάασκε is an iterative of ναιετάω ‘dwell’. ῥύσι’ ἐλαυνόμενος, ‘driving off goods taken in reprisal’, belongs with ἐγώ, the subject of κτάνον (an unaugmented aorist): Nestor was the one driving, ῥύσια being goods seized to make good a debt, which the passage explains from 686 on.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἀμύνων ᾗσι βόεσσιν
ἔβλητ’ ἐν πρώτοισιν ἐμῆς ἀπὸ χειρὸς ἄκοντι,
κὰδ δ’ ἔπεσεν, λαοὶ δὲ περίτρεσαν ἀγροιῶται.
sentences.l:
and he, defending his own cattle,
was struck among the foremost by a javelin from my hand,
and fell down, and the people trembled all round, the countrymen.
sentences.i: and he, defending his own cattle, was struck among the foremost by a javelin from my hand and fell, and the countrymen all round flinched in fear.
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ ‘and he’ is Itymoneus. ᾗσι is the possessive ‘his own’, not the relative, and βόεσσιν is the epic dative plural of βοῦς. ἔβλητ’ is ἔβλητο, the epic passive aorist of βάλλω, ‘was struck’, by a javelin (ἄκοντι), and ἐν πρώτοισιν is ‘among the foremost’. κὰδ δ’ ἔπεσεν is κατὰ … ἔπεσεν ‘fell down’ with κατά shortened and assimilated. περίτρεσαν is ‘trembled all round’, said of the countrymen (ἀγροιῶται).

sentences.t:
ληΐδα δ’ ἐκ πεδίου συνελάσσαμεν ἤλιθα πολλὴν
πεντήκοντα βοῶν ἀγέλας, τόσα πώεα οἰῶν,
τόσσα συῶν συβόσια, τόσ’ αἰπόλια πλατέ’ αἰγῶν,
sentences.l:
And spoil from the plain we drove together, exceeding much:
fifty herds of cattle, as many flocks of sheep,
as many droves of swine, as many wide herds of goats,
sentences.i: and from the plain we drove together a very great spoil: fifty herds of cattle, as many flocks of sheep, as many droves of swine, as many wide herds of goats,
sentences.n: The spoil is counted in a list with no verb of its own. ληΐδα ‘spoil’ is the object of συνελάσσαμεν ‘we drove together’ (συνελαύνω, with the doubled σ), and ἤλιθα πολλήν is ‘exceeding much’. Fifty herds (ἀγέλας) of cattle are named, then τόσα ‘as many’ flocks (πώεα) of sheep, droves (συβόσια) of swine and herds (αἰπόλια) of goats. The second half of 678 and all of 679 also stand in the Odyssey (14.100–101), and their English is the Odyssey’s.

sentences.t:
ἵππους δὲ ξανθὰς ἑκατὸν καὶ πεντήκοντα
πάσας θηλείας, πολλῇσι δὲ πῶλοι ὑπῆσαν.
sentences.l:
and horses, chestnut, a hundred and fifty,
all female, and under many were foals.
sentences.i: and a hundred and fifty chestnut horses, all of them mares, and many had foals beneath them.
sentences.n: ἵππους is the accusative plural, the same form for stallions and mares, but ξανθάς ‘chestnut’ is feminine, because the horses are mares, and the next line says so (πάσας θηλείας ‘all female’). ξανθός is a colour word, ‘yellowish, chestnut’; elsewhere the translation gives it as ‘fair-haired’ of people. πολλῇσι is the epic dative plural ‘to many’, and ὑπῆσαν ‘were underneath’ means that many mares had foals (πῶλοι) at their sides.

sentences.t:
καὶ τὰ μὲν ἠλασάμεσθα Πύλον Νηλήϊον εἴσω
ἐννύχιοι προτὶ ἄστυ·
sentences.l:
And these we drove into Neleian Pylos,
by night, to the town;
sentences.i: These we drove by night into Neleian Pylos, to the town;
sentences.n: τὰ μὲν ‘these’ are the cattle and the rest of the spoil. Πύλον Νηλήϊον is ‘Pylos of Neleus’, Νηλήϊος being the adjective from Νηλεύς, and εἴσω ‘into’ governs it. ἠλασάμεσθα is the aorist middle of ἐλαύνω ‘drive’, ‘we drove for ourselves’, with the ending -μεσθα. ἐννύχιοι is an adjective used as an adverb, ‘by night’, agreeing with the subject.

sentences.t:
γεγήθει δὲ φρένα Νηλεύς,
οὕνεκά μοι τύχε πολλὰ νέῳ πόλεμον δὲ κιόντι.
sentences.l:
and Neleus was glad in his wits,
because many things fell to me, young, as I was going to war.
sentences.i: and Neleus was glad in his mind, because much had come my way while I was young and going to war.
sentences.n: γεγήθει is the pluperfect of γηθέω ‘rejoice’, used as a plain past tense, and φρένα is an accusative of respect, ‘glad in his wits’ (the English says ‘mind’). οὕνεκα is ‘because’. τύχε is the unaugmented aorist of τυγχάνω ‘happen, fall to’, so ‘many things fell to me’; νέῳ ‘young’ agrees with μοι, and πόλεμον δέ ‘to war’ has the direction-ending -δε.

sentences.t:
κήρυκες δ’ ἐλίγαινον ἅμ’ ἠοῖ φαινομένηφι
τοὺς ἴμεν οἷσι χρεῖος ὀφείλετ’ ἐν Ἤλιδι δίῃ·
sentences.l:
And heralds cried out clearly with dawn appearing
that those should go to whom a debt was owed in heavenly Elis;
sentences.i: At first light the heralds cried out clearly that all those to whom a debt was owed in heavenly Elis should go;
sentences.n: κήρυκες ‘heralds’ make a proclamation. ἐλίγαινον is the imperfect of λιγαίνω ‘cry out in a clear voice’, from λιγύς ‘clear’. ἅμ’ ἠοῖ φαινομένηφι is ‘with dawn appearing’, φαινομένηφι having the old ending -φι, so ‘at first light’. τοὺς ἴμεν is ‘that those should go’, ἴμεν being the epic infinitive of εἶμι; οἷσι χρεῖος ὀφείλετ’ is ‘to whom a debt was owed’. δίῃ ‘heavenly’ is the epithet of Elis.

sentences.t:
οἳ δὲ συναγρόμενοι Πυλίων ἡγήτορες ἄνδρες
δαίτρευον·
sentences.l:
And they, gathering together, the leaders of the Pylians, men,
made the division;
sentences.i: The leaders of the Pylians gathered together and made the division;
sentences.n: οἳ δέ ‘and they’ begins a new sentence. συναγρόμενοι is the aorist middle participle of συναγείρω ‘gather together’, with the epic syncopated form. Πυλίων ἡγήτορες ἄνδρες is ‘the leaders of the Pylians, men’, the second noun in apposition. δαίτρευον is the imperfect of δαιτρεύω ‘divide into portions’, from the same root as δαίς ‘feast’; the sharing out of what was owed begins here.

sentences.t:
πολέσιν γὰρ Ἐπειοὶ χρεῖος ὄφειλον,
ὡς ἡμεῖς παῦροι κεκακωμένοι ἐν Πύλῳ ἦμεν·
sentences.l:
for to many the Epeans owed a debt,
since we were few, ill-treated, in Pylos;
sentences.i: for the Epeans owed a debt to many, since we in Pylos were few and had been ill-treated;
sentences.n: πολέσιν is the epic dative plural of πολύς, ‘to many’, and χρεῖος ὄφειλον is ‘owed a debt’, the Epeans being the debtors. ὡς … ἦμεν is ‘since we were’, ὡς used causally: Pylos was weak, so many Pylians were owed. κεκακωμένοι is the perfect passive participle of κακόω ‘ill-treat’, and παῦροι is ‘few’; the verb returns as ἐκάκωσε in the next line.

sentences.t:
ἐλθὼν γάρ ῥ’ ἐκάκωσε βίη Ἡρακληείη
τῶν προτέρων ἐτέων, κατὰ δ’ ἔκταθεν ὅσσοι ἄριστοι·
sentences.l:
For coming, the might of Heracles ill-treated us
in the former years, and all who were the best were killed;
sentences.i: For the might of Heracles came and ill-treated us in the years before, and all who were the best were killed;
sentences.n: ἐλθὼν … ἐκάκωσε ‘coming, ill-treated’ explains κεκακωμένοι. The subject, βίη Ἡρακληείη, is literally ‘the might of Heracles’, a periphrasis for Heracles himself, which the English keeps; ῥ’ is ῥα, a particle. τῶν προτέρων ἐτέων is a genitive of time, ‘in the former years’. κατὰ … ἔκταθεν is tmesis: ἔκταθεν is the epic passive aorist of κτείνω ‘kill’, ‘were killed’, and ὅσσοι ἄριστοι is ‘all who were the best’.

sentences.t: δώδεκα γὰρ Νηλῆος ἀμύμονος υἱέες ἦμεν·
sentences.l: for twelve sons of Neleus, the blameless, were we;
sentences.i: for we were twelve sons of blameless Neleus;
sentences.n: γάρ gives the reason for the weakness of Pylos. δώδεκα … υἱέες ἦμεν is ‘we were twelve sons’, υἱέες being the nominative plural of υἱός. Νηλῆος is the Homeric genitive of Νηλεύς. ἀμύμονος ‘blameless’ is the stock epithet; the exact sense of ἀμύμων was already uncertain, and its original meaning is not known.

sentences.t: τῶν οἶος λιπόμην, οἳ δ’ ἄλλοι πάντες ὄλοντο.
sentences.l: of these I alone was left behind, and the others all perished.
sentences.i: of them I alone was left behind, and all the others perished.
sentences.n: τῶν is a partitive genitive, ‘of these’, and οἶος is ‘alone’. λιπόμην is the aorist middle of λείπω in a passive sense, ‘was left behind’. ὄλοντο is the unaugmented aorist middle of ὄλλυμι ‘destroy’ (Attic ὠλόμην), so ‘perished’. The line says that of the twelve brothers Nestor alone survived the earlier war with Heracles.

sentences.t:
ταῦθ’ ὑπερηφανέοντες Ἐπειοὶ χαλκοχίτωνες
ἡμέας ὑβρίζοντες ἀτάσθαλα μηχανόωντο.
sentences.l:
In these matters, behaving overbearingly, the bronze-shirted Epeans,
behaving insolently to us, devised wanton things.
sentences.i: Overbearing in this, the bronze-shirted Epeans treated us with insolence and devised wanton deeds.
sentences.n: ταῦθ’ is ταῦτα, ‘in these matters’, and ὑπερηφανέοντες ‘behaving overbearingly’ is built on ὑπερήφανος with the open epic ending -έοντες (Attic -οῦντες). χαλκοχίτωνες ‘bronze-shirted’ is the epithet the translation gives to the Achaeans elsewhere, here used of the Epeans. ὑβρίζοντες is ‘behaving with insolence’ (ὕβρις), and ἀτάσθαλα μηχανόωντο is ‘devised wanton things’, with the open form of μηχανῶντο.

sentences.t:
ἐκ δ’ ὃ γέρων ἀγέλην τε βοῶν καὶ πῶϋ μέγ’ οἰῶν
εἵλετο κρινάμενος τριηκόσι’ ἠδὲ νομῆας.
sentences.l:
And out the old man a herd of cattle and a great flock of sheep
took, picking three hundred, and herdsmen too.
sentences.i: The old man took out a herd of cattle and a great flock of sheep, picking out three hundred head, and herdsmen too.
sentences.n: ὃ γέρων ‘the old man’ is Neleus, named at 692. ἐκ … εἵλετο is tmesis, ‘took out’. ἀγέλην … βοῶν is ‘a herd of cattle’ and πῶϋ … οἰῶν ‘a flock of sheep’, with μέγ’ ‘great’. κρινάμενος ‘picking out’ goes with τριηκόσι’ ‘three hundred’ (head), and νομῆας ‘herdsmen’ come with them. What he takes is not the spoil of 677–681 but payment of what was owed him in Elis, told in the next lines.

sentences.t:
καὶ γὰρ τῷ χρεῖος μέγ’ ὀφείλετ’ ἐν Ἤλιδι δίῃ
τέσσαρες ἀθλοφόροι ἵπποι αὐτοῖσιν ὄχεσφιν
ἐλθόντες μετ’ ἄεθλα·
sentences.i: For he too was owed a great debt in heavenly Elis: four prize-bearing horses, chariots and all, that had gone to the contests;
sentences.n: καὶ γὰρ τῷ ‘for to him too’ begins a second debt owed to Neleus. ἀθλοφόροι ‘prize-bearing’ is built on ἆθλον and φέρω ‘carry’. αὐτοῖσιν ὄχεσφιν is ‘with the very chariots’: ὄχεσφιν has the old instrumental ending -φιν, and ὄχεα are chariots. μετ’ ἄεθλα is ‘to the contests’, ἄεθλα being the open form of ἆθλα, which can also mean ‘prizes’. The horses are the debt, and the next lines say why they had come and what Augeias then did.

sentences.t:
περὶ τρίποδος γὰρ ἔμελλον
θεύσεσθαι·
sentences.l:
for about a tripod they were going
to run;
sentences.i: for they were to run for a tripod;
sentences.n: περὶ τρίποδος γὰρ ἔμελλον θεύσεσθαι gives the reason for the horses’ journey. A τρίπους is a three-legged cauldron, a valued prize. ἔμελλον with the future infinitive θεύσεσθαι (from θέω ‘run’) is ‘were going to run’, and περί with the genitive means ‘for’ the prize being competed for.

sentences.t:
τοὺς δ’ αὖθι ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Αὐγείας
κάσχεθε, τὸν δ’ ἐλατῆρ’ ἀφίει ἀκαχήμενον ἵππων.
sentences.l:
but them on the spot the lord of men Augeias
held back, and the driver he let go, grieved for his horses.
sentences.i: but Augeias, lord of men, kept them there, and let the driver go, grieved for his horses.
sentences.n: τοὺς … κάσχεθε ‘held them back’: κάσχεθε is κατέσχεθε with the preverb shortened, the aorist of κατέχω. Αὐγείας is Augeias, who is named again at 739. ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν ‘lord of men’ is the phrase the translation also gives Agamemnon, used here of Augeias. τὸν δ’ ἐλατῆρ’ is ‘and the driver’, ἐλατήρ being the man who drives the chariot. ἀκαχήμενον ἵππων is ‘grieved for the horses’, ἵππων a genitive of the thing grieved for.

sentences.t:
τῶν ὃ γέρων ἐπέων κεχολωμένος ἠδὲ καὶ ἔργων
ἐξέλετ’ ἄσπετα πολλά·
sentences.l:
At these words and deeds the old man, angered,
took out boundless, many things;
sentences.i: Angered at those words and deeds, the old man took out a boundless amount;
sentences.n: τῶν ἐπέων … ἔργων ‘at those words and deeds’ points back to Augeias’ treatment of the horses and their driver. κεχολωμένος is the perfect passive participle of χολόω ‘anger’, from χόλος ‘anger’. ἐξέλετ’ is ἐξείλετο ‘took out for himself’, and ἄσπετα πολλά is ‘boundless, many things’, ἄσπετος meaning literally ‘not to be told’.

sentences.t:
τὰ δ’ ἄλλ’ ἐς δῆμον ἔδωκε
δαιτρεύειν, μή τίς οἱ ἀτεμβόμενος κίοι ἴσης.
sentences.l:
and the rest to the people he gave
to divide, so that no one, for him, cheated, should go off short of an equal share.
sentences.i: and the rest he gave to the people to divide, so that no one, on his account, should go away cheated of an equal share.
sentences.n: τὰ δ’ ἄλλ’ ‘and the rest’ is what Neleus did not keep. δῆμος here is the common people, not the army (λαός), and δαιτρεύειν ‘to divide’ is an infinitive of purpose. μή τίς οἱ … κίοι ἴσης is a negative purpose clause with the optative, ‘so that no one … should’: ἀτεμβόμενος ‘cheated’ goes with τίς ‘anyone’, ἴσης is a genitive of separation, ‘short of an equal share’, and οἱ ‘for him’ is Neleus, a dative of interest. The same clause stands at Odyssey 9.42 and 9.549, and its English is theirs.

sentences.t:
ἡμεῖς μὲν τὰ ἕκαστα διείπομεν, ἀμφί τε ἄστυ
ἕρδομεν ἱρὰ θεοῖς·
sentences.l:
We then arranged each of these matters, and around the town
performed sacrifices to the gods;
sentences.i: We settled each of these matters, and around the town we performed sacrifices to the gods;
sentences.n: ἡμεῖς μέν ‘we, for our part’ contrasts Nestor’s people with the Epeans, who come in the next sentence. τὰ ἕκαστα is ‘each of the matters’, one by one, and διείπομεν is ‘we arranged, settled’, from διά ‘through’ and εἶπον ‘say’. ἕρδομεν ‘we performed’ is from ἕρδω, another verb for ῥέζω ‘do, perform’, and ἱρά is the Ionic ἱερά ‘sacrifices’. ἀμφί … ἄστυ is ‘around the town’.

sentences.t:
οἳ δὲ τρίτῳ ἤματι πάντες
ἦλθον ὁμῶς αὐτοί τε πολεῖς καὶ μώνυχες ἵπποι
πανσυδίῃ· μετὰ δέ σφι Μολίονε θωρήσσοντο
παῖδ’ ἔτ’ ἐόντ’, οὔ πω μάλα εἰδότε θούριδος ἀλκῆς.
sentences.l:
And they on the third day, all,
came alike, themselves many and solid-hoofed horses,
with-all-rush; and with them the two Molions were arming themselves,
still being boys, not yet well knowing impetuous might.
sentences.i: And on the third day they all came together, many men and solid-hoofed horses alike, with all speed; and with them the two Molions were arming themselves, still boys, not yet well versed in impetuous might.
sentences.n: οἳ δέ ‘and they’ are the Epeans. πολεῖς is the Ionic nominative plural of πολύς ‘many’; μώνυχες ‘solid-hoofed’ is the epithet of horses; πανσυδίῃ ‘with all speed’ is built from πᾶς and σεύομαι ‘rush’. Μολίονε is a dual, ‘the two Molions’, a pair of boys, and θωρήσσοντο is ‘were arming themselves’. εἰδότε is the dual participle of οἶδα ‘know’, with θούριδος ἀλκῆς ‘impetuous might’ in the genitive.

sentences.t:
ἔστι δέ τις Θρυόεσσα πόλις αἰπεῖα κολώνη
τηλοῦ ἐπ’ Ἀλφειῷ, νεάτη Πύλου ἠμαθόεντος·
τὴν ἀμφεστρατόωντο διαρραῖσαι μεμαῶτες.
sentences.i: There is a city, Thryoessa, on a steep hill, far off on the Alpheus, at the farthest edge of sandy Pylos; they camped around it, eager to raze it.
sentences.n: Θρυόεσσα is a place name, and αἰπεῖα κολώνη ‘a steep hill’ stands in apposition to πόλις ‘city’, so the city sits on a height. τηλοῦ ἐπ’ Ἀλφειῷ is ‘far off on the Alpheus’, and νεάτη Πύλου ἠμαθόεντος ‘the furthest of sandy Pylos’ gives its place at the edge of Nestor’s country. ἀμφεστρατόωντο is the imperfect of ἀμφιστρατάομαι ‘encamp around’, and διαρραῖσαι ‘to raze’ is the infinitive that μεμαῶτες ‘eager’ governs.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε πᾶν πεδίον μετεκίαθον, ἄμμι δ’ Ἀθήνη
ἄγγελος ἦλθε θέουσ’ ἀπ’ Ὀλύμπου θωρήσσεσθαι
ἔννυχος,
sentences.l:
But when they had traversed the whole plain, to us Athena
came as a messenger, running from Olympus, to arm,
in the night,
sentences.i: But when they had crossed the whole plain, Athena came to us as a messenger, running from Olympus in the night, to have us arm,
sentences.n: The subject of μετεκίαθον, ‘they had traversed’, is still the Epeans of 713, who have crossed the plain to reach Thryoessa. ἄμμι is the epic dative ‘to us’ (Attic ἡμῖν). Ἀθήνη ἄγγελος is ‘Athena as a messenger’; θέουσ’ is the participle of θέω ‘run’, and θωρήσσεσθαι ‘to arm’ is an infinitive of purpose, the content of her message. ἔννυχος ‘in the night’ is an adjective used as an adverb.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἀέκοντα Πύλον κάτα λαὸν ἄγειρεν
ἀλλὰ μάλ’ ἐσσυμένους πολεμίζειν.
sentences.l:
and not unwilling the people throughout Pylos she gathered,
but very eager to fight.
sentences.i: She gathered the troops throughout Pylos, not unwilling but very eager to fight.
sentences.n: ἄγειρεν is the imperfect of ἀγείρω ‘gather’, and Πύλον κάτα is ‘throughout Pylos’, κάτα being κατά placed after its noun. λαόν ‘the people’ is singular, and so is ἀέκοντα ‘unwilling’, but ἐσσυμένους ‘eager’ is plural: the Greek moves from the people as one body to the men who make it up. οὐδ’ … ἀλλά is ‘not … but’.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ με Νηλεὺς
εἴα θωρήσσεσθαι, ἀπέκρυψεν δέ μοι ἵππους·
οὐ γάρ πώ τί μ’ ἔφη ἴδμεν πολεμήϊα ἔργα.
sentences.i: But Neleus would not let me arm, and hid my horses from me, for he said I did not yet know anything of the deeds of war.
sentences.n: Neleus keeps the young Nestor at home. οὐδέ με … εἴα is ‘did not allow me’, εἴα being the imperfect of ἐάω, with θωρήσσεσθαι ‘to arm’. ἀπέκρυψεν … μοι ἵππους is ‘hid the horses from me’. In οὐ γάρ πώ τί μ’ ἔφη ἴδμεν, ἴδμεν is the epic infinitive of οἶδα ‘know’, so ‘he said I knew nothing yet’, and πολεμήϊα ἔργα is ‘the works of war’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ καὶ ὧς ἱππεῦσι μετέπρεπον ἡμετέροισι
καὶ πεζός περ ἐών, ἐπεὶ ὧς ἄγε νεῖκος Ἀθήνη.
sentences.l:
But even so I was conspicuous among our horsemen,
even though being on foot, since in this way Athena led the quarrel.
sentences.i: But even so I was conspicuous among our horsemen, though I was on foot, since that was how Athena led the quarrel.
sentences.n: ἱππεῦσι … ἡμετέροισι is ‘among our horsemen’, and μετέπρεπον, the imperfect of μεταπρέπω, is ‘was conspicuous among’. καὶ πεζός περ ἐών is ‘even though being on foot’: περ makes the participle concessive. ἐπεὶ ὧς ἄγε νεῖκος Ἀθήνη is ‘since so Athena led the quarrel’; ἄγε is the unaugmented imperfect of ἄγω, and νεῖκος ‘quarrel’ is the word for the whole conflict.

sentences.t:
ἔστι δέ τις ποταμὸς Μινυήϊος εἰς ἅλα βάλλων
ἐγγύθεν Ἀρήνης, ὅθι μείναμεν Ἠῶ δῖαν
ἱππῆες Πυλίων, τὰ δ’ ἐπέρρεον ἔθνεα πεζῶν.
sentences.l:
And there is a certain river Minyeïus, falling into the sea
near Arene, where we waited for heavenly Dawn,
the horsemen of the Pylians, and the tribes of men on foot flowed up.
sentences.i: There is a river Minyeïus that falls into the sea near Arene, where we, the horsemen of the Pylians, waited for heavenly Dawn, while the bands of men on foot flowed up.
sentences.n: Μινυήϊος is the adjective ‘Minyeïan’ used as the river’s name; εἰς ἅλα βάλλων is ‘falling into the sea’, with ἅλα the accusative of ἅλς. Ἀρήνη is a town named only as a landmark. Ἠῶ δῖαν is ‘heavenly Dawn’. ἱππῆες Πυλίων ‘the horsemen of the Pylians’ are the subject of μείναμεν ‘we waited’. τὰ δ’ ‘and those’ introduces ἔθνεα πεζῶν ‘the tribes of men on foot’, which ἐπέρρεον ‘flowed up’ like water.

sentences.t:
ἔνθεν πανσυδίῃ σὺν τεύχεσι θωρηχθέντες
ἔνδιοι ἱκόμεσθ’ ἱερὸν ῥόον Ἀλφειοῖο.
sentences.l:
From there, with-all-rush, with our armour armed,
at midday we came to the sacred stream of the Alpheus.
sentences.i: From there, with all speed, armed in our armour, we came at midday to the sacred stream of the Alpheus.
sentences.n: ἔνθεν is ‘from there’. πανσυδίῃ ‘with all speed’ recurs from 709. σὺν τεύχεσι θωρηχθέντες is ‘armed in our armour’, the passive aorist participle of θωρήσσω, the verb of 715. ἔνδιοι ‘at midday’ is an adjective used as an adverb, and ἱκόμεσθ’ is ἱκόμεθα ‘we reached’ with the ending -μεσθα. ἱερὸν ῥόον Ἀλφειοῖο is ‘the sacred stream of the Alpheus’, a river that receives a sacrifice in the next lines.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα Διὶ ῥέξαντες ὑπερμενεῖ ἱερὰ καλά,
ταῦρον δ’ Ἀλφειῷ, ταῦρον δὲ Ποσειδάωνι,
αὐτὰρ Ἀθηναίη γλαυκώπιδι βοῦν ἀγελαίην,
sentences.l:
There, having performed to exceeding-strong Zeus fine sacrifices,
a bull to the Alpheus, and a bull to Poseidon,
and to Athena, gleaming-eyed, a cow of the herd,
sentences.i: There, having made fine sacrifices to Zeus of surpassing strength, a bull to the Alpheus, a bull to Poseidon, and to gleaming-eyed Athena a cow from the herd,
sentences.n: ῥέξαντες is the aorist participle of ῥέζω ‘perform’, with ἱερὰ καλά ‘fine sacrifices’ as its object; the victims follow in apposition, so the river Alpheus receives a bull as a god does. ὑπερμενεῖ ‘exceeding-strong’ is Zeus’ epithet here. Ἀθηναίῃ is the Ionic dative, γλαυκώπιδι ‘gleaming-eyed’ is her stock epithet, whose exact sense is a guess, and βοῦν ἀγελαίην is ‘a cow of the herd’.

sentences.t:
δόρπον ἔπειθ’ ἑλόμεσθα κατὰ στρατὸν ἐν τελέεσσι,
καὶ κατεκοιμήθημεν ἐν ἔντεσιν οἷσιν ἕκαστος
ἀμφὶ ῥοὰς ποταμοῖο.
sentences.l:
supper then we took throughout the army, in companies,
and we lay down to sleep, each in his own gear,
about the streams of the river.
sentences.i: Then we took our supper through the army, company by company, and lay down to sleep, each in his own gear, beside the streams of the river.
sentences.n: δόρπον … ἑλόμεσθα is ‘we took supper’, ἑλόμεσθα being the epic ἑλόμεθα, the aorist middle of αἱρέω. ἐν τελέεσσι is ‘in companies’ (τέλεα, a body of troops), and κατὰ στρατόν ‘throughout the army’. κατεκοιμήθημεν is ‘we lay down to sleep’; οἷσιν is the possessive ‘his own’, with ἕκαστος ‘each’. ἀμφὶ ῥοὰς ποταμοῖο is ‘about the streams of the river’, ῥοάς being the accusative plural of ῥοή.

sentences.t:
ἀτὰρ μεγάθυμοι Ἐπειοὶ
ἀμφέσταν δὴ ἄστυ διαρραῖσαι μεμαῶτες·
sentences.l:
But the great-hearted Epeans
had by now taken their stand about the town, eager to raze it;
sentences.i: But the great-hearted Epeans had by now taken their stand around the town, eager to raze it;
sentences.n: ἀτὰρ marks the contrast with the Pylians sleeping by the river. μεγάθυμοι ‘great-hearted’ is the stock epithet. ἀμφέσταν is ἀμφέστησαν, the intransitive aorist of ἀμφίστημι, ‘stood around’, and δὴ ἄστυ ‘by now … the town’ is the πόλις of 711. διαρραῖσαι μεμαῶτες repeats the end of 713.

sentences.t: ἀλλά σφι προπάροιθε φάνη μέγα ἔργον Ἄρηος·
sentences.l: but before them appeared a great work of Ares;
sentences.i: but a great work of Ares appeared before them;
sentences.n: σφι is the dative ‘to them’, the Epeans, and προπάροιθε ‘before them’ is a preposition-like adverb. φάνη is the passive aorist of φαίνω, used like a middle, ‘appeared’. ἔργον Ἄρηος ‘a work of Ares’ is battle, the god’s name standing for war; Ἄρηος is the epic genitive of Ἄρης.

sentences.t:
εὖτε γὰρ ἠέλιος φαέθων ὑπερέσχεθε γαίης,
συμφερόμεσθα μάχῃ Διί τ’ εὐχόμενοι καὶ Ἀθήνῃ.
sentences.l:
For when the shining sun held itself above the earth,
we clashed in battle, praying to Zeus and to Athena.
sentences.i: For when the shining sun rose above the earth, we met in battle, praying to Zeus and to Athena.
sentences.n: εὖτε γάρ ‘for when’ gives the time. ἠέλιος φαέθων is ‘the shining sun’, φαέθων being the stock epithet. ὑπερέσχεθε γαίης is ‘held itself above the earth’, i.e. rose: the aorist of ὑπερέχω, with the genitive. συμφερόμεσθα is the unaugmented imperfect of συμφέρομαι ‘come together’ in a fight, μάχῃ ‘in battle’. Διί τ’ εὐχόμενοι καὶ Ἀθήνῃ is ‘praying to Zeus and to Athena’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ Πυλίων καὶ Ἐπειῶν ἔπλετο νεῖκος,
πρῶτος ἐγὼν ἕλον ἄνδρα, κόμισσα δὲ μώνυχας ἵππους,
Μούλιον αἰχμητήν·
sentences.i: But when the quarrel arose between the Pylians and the Epeans, I was the first to take a man, and I took charge of his solid-hoofed horses: Mulius, the spearman;
sentences.n: ἔπλετο is the epic aorist of πέλομαι ‘become’, so ‘the quarrel arose’. ἐγών is the epic ἐγώ. ἕλον is the aorist of αἱρέω, ‘took’ and here ‘killed’. κόμισσα … ἵππους is ‘I took charge of the horses’, the horses of the man just killed; κομίζω is ‘take care of, carry off’. Μούλιον αἰχμητήν is ‘Mulius the spearman’, in the accusative with ἄνδρα; the sentence breaks at ·, and the next one says who he was.

sentences.t:
γαμβρὸς δ’ ἦν Αὐγείαο,
πρεσβυτάτην δὲ θύγατρ’ εἶχε ξανθὴν Ἀγαμήδην,
ἣ τόσα φάρμακα ᾔδη ὅσα τρέφει εὐρεῖα χθών.
sentences.l:
and he was son-in-law of Augeias,
and the eldest daughter he had, fair-haired Agamede,
who knew as many drugs as the wide earth nourishes.
sentences.i: He was a son-in-law of Augeias, and had as wife the eldest daughter, fair-haired Agamede, who knew as many drugs as the wide earth nourishes.
sentences.n: γαμβρός is a daughter’s husband, ‘son-in-law’, and Αὐγείαο is the epic genitive of Αὐγείας. πρεσβυτάτην … θύγατρ’ εἶχε is ‘had the eldest daughter’ (as wife). ξανθήν is ‘fair-haired’, the translation’s word for ξανθός of people. ἣ τόσα φάρμακα ᾔδη ὅσα … is ‘who knew as many drugs as’: ᾔδη is the pluperfect of οἶδα used as a past tense, and τρέφει εὐρεῖα χθών ‘the wide earth nourishes’ names the earth as the source of the herbs.

sentences.t:
τὸν μὲν ἐγὼ προσιόντα βάλον χαλκήρεϊ δουρί,
ἤριπε δ’ ἐν κονίῃσιν·
sentences.l:
Him, as he came on, I struck with my bronze-fitted spear,
and he crashed down in the dust;
sentences.i: I struck him as he came on with my bronze-fitted spear, and he crashed down in the dust;
sentences.n: τὸν μέν ‘him’ is Mulius. βάλον is the unaugmented aorist of βάλλω ‘strike’, and προσιόντα ‘as he came on’ is a participle of πρόσειμι. χαλκήρεϊ δουρί is ‘with a bronze-fitted spear’, the spear with its bronze head fitted on. ἤριπε ‘crashed down’ is the aorist of ἐρείπω, and ἐν κονίῃσιν is ‘in the dust’ with the plural of κονία.

sentences.t:
ἐγὼ δ’ ἐς δίφρον ὀρούσας
στῆν ῥα μετὰ προμάχοισιν·
sentences.l:
and I, having sprung into the chariot,
stood among the front-fighters;
sentences.i: and I sprang into my chariot and took my stand among the foremost fighters;
sentences.n: ἐς δίφρον ὀρούσας is ‘having sprung into the chariot’ (ὀρούω ‘rush, spring’; δίφρος is the chariot or its floor). στῆν is ἔστην ‘I stood’ without the augment, and ῥα is the particle. μετὰ προμάχοισιν is ‘among the front-fighters’, προμάχοισι being the men in the front rank.

sentences.t:
ἀτὰρ μεγάθυμοι Ἐπειοὶ
ἔτρεσαν ἄλλυδις ἄλλος, ἐπεὶ ἴδον ἄνδρα πεσόντα
ἡγεμόν’ ἱππήων, ὃς ἀριστεύεσκε μάχεσθαι.
sentences.l:
but the great-hearted Epeans
trembled, one this way, one that, when they saw the man fallen,
the leader of the horsemen, who used to be the best at fighting.
sentences.i: and the great-hearted Epeans flinched and scattered, one this way and one that, when they saw the man fallen, the leader of the horsemen, who used to be the best at fighting.
sentences.n: ἔτρεσαν is from τρέω, the verb for trembling and shrinking back, and ἄλλυδις ἄλλος ‘one this way, one that’ shows the scattering. ἴδον ἄνδρα πεσόντα is ‘saw the man fallen’, with the aorist participle of πίπτω. ἡγεμόν’ ἱππήων is ‘the leader of the horsemen’, ἱππήων the epic genitive of ἱππεύς. ὃς ἀριστεύεσκε μάχεσθαι is ‘who used to be the best at fighting’, the ending -σκε marking repeated action.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼν ἐπόρουσα κελαινῇ λαίλαπι ἶσος,
πεντήκοντα δ’ ἕλον δίφρους, δύο δ’ ἀμφὶς ἕκαστον
φῶτες ὀδὰξ ἕλον οὖδας ἐμῷ ὑπὸ δουρὶ δαμέντες.
sentences.l:
But I rushed upon them like a dark squall,
and fifty chariots I took, and about each two
men with their teeth bit the ground, subdued under my spear.
sentences.i: I rushed on them like a dark squall and took fifty chariots, and two men for each of them bit the earth with their teeth, brought down under my spear.
sentences.n: The comparison is packed into a phrase: κελαινῇ λαίλαπι ἶσος ‘like a dark squall’. ἐπόρουσα is the aorist of ἐπορούω ‘rush upon’. πεντήκοντα δ’ ἕλον δίφρους is ‘I took fifty chariots’, and δύο … φῶτες ‘two men’ stand ἀμφὶς ἕκαστον ‘around each’. ὀδὰξ ἕλον οὖδας is ‘bit the ground with their teeth’, a way of saying they fell dying, and δαμέντες is the passive aorist participle of δάμνημι ‘subdue’.

sentences.t:
καί νύ κεν Ἀκτορίωνε Μολίονε παῖδ’ ἀλάπαξα,
εἰ μή σφωε πατὴρ εὐρὺ κρείων ἐνοσίχθων
ἐκ πολέμου ἐσάωσε καλύψας ἠέρι πολλῇ.
sentences.l:
And now indeed the two of Actor’s line, the Molions, as boys I would have laid waste,
had not their father, wide-ruling earth-shaker,
saved them from the war, having covered them in thick mist.
sentences.i: And then I would have laid waste the pair of Actor’s line, the Molions, boys though they were, had not their father, the wide-ruling earth-shaker, saved them from the war by covering them in thick mist.
sentences.n: καί νύ κεν … ἀλάπαξα is a past unreal condition: ‘I would have laid waste’, with the condition in εἰ μή ‘if not’, 751. Ἀκτορίωνε Μολίονε are two names in the dual for the same pair: Ἀκτορίωνε is a patronymic, ‘the two of Actor’s line’, and Μολίονε is ‘the two Molions’, the name they are best known by. εὐρὺ κρείων is ‘wide-ruling’ (printed as two words) and ἐνοσίχθων ‘earth-shaker’ is the stock epithet of Poseidon, who is not named; the Greek calls him their πατήρ. ἠέρι πολλῇ is ‘thick mist’.

sentences.t: ἔνθα Ζεὺς Πυλίοισι μέγα κράτος ἐγγυάλιξε·
sentences.l: Then Zeus to the Pylians great strength put into their hands;
sentences.i: Then Zeus put great strength into the hands of the Pylians;
sentences.n: ἔνθα ‘then’ marks the turn of the fight. ἐγγυάλιξε is the aorist of ἐγγυαλίζω ‘put into the hands’. κράτος is ‘strength’, the house rendering, with the sense of the upper hand included; Πυλίοισι is the epic dative plural of Πύλιοι.

sentences.t:
τόφρα γὰρ οὖν ἑπόμεσθα διὰ σπιδέος πεδίοιο
κτείνοντές τ’ αὐτοὺς ἀνά τ’ ἔντεα καλὰ λέγοντες,
sentences.l:
For that time indeed we followed across the broad plain,
killing the men themselves and gathering up the fine gear,
sentences.i: For all that time we followed them across the broad plain, killing the men themselves and gathering up the fine gear,
sentences.n: τόφρα … ὄφρ’ ‘for that time … until’ frame the pursuit, and the ὄφρ’ clause begins in the next unit. οὖν ‘indeed’ is a connecting particle, and ἑπόμεσθα is the imperfect of ἕπομαι ‘follow’. διὰ σπιδέος πεδίοιο is ‘across the broad plain’, σπιδής meaning ‘wide’. The participles κτείνοντες ‘killing’ and ἀνὰ … λέγοντες ‘gathering up’ (tmesis) say what the following consisted of.

sentences.t:
ὄφρ’ ἐπὶ Βουπρασίου πολυπύρου βήσαμεν ἵππους
πέτρης τ’ Ὠλενίης, καὶ Ἀλησίου ἔνθα κολώνη
κέκληται·
sentences.i: until we brought our horses to Buprasium, rich in wheat, and to the Olenian rock, and to the place called the hill of Alesium;
sentences.n: ὄφρ’ ‘until’ completes τόφρα of the line before. βήσαμεν ἵππους is ‘we made the horses go’, the causative aorist of βαίνω, ‘drove’. Βουπρασίου πολυπύρου is ‘Buprasium rich in wheat’, πολύπυρος meaning ‘of much wheat’. Three places mark the end of the chase: Buprasium, the rock πέτρης … Ὠλενίης, and the hill that Ἀλησίου … κολώνη κέκληται ‘is called Alesium’s’, κέκληται being the perfect passive of καλέω.

sentences.t: ὅθεν αὖτις ἀπέτραπε λαὸν Ἀθήνη.
sentences.l: from where again turned back the people Athena.
sentences.i: and from there Athena turned the troops back.
sentences.n: ὅθεν ‘from where’ looks back to the places just named, and αὖτις is ‘again, back’. ἀπέτραπε is the aorist of ἀποτρέπω ‘turn away’, here ‘turned back’, and λαόν is the army. Ἀθήνη stands at the end of the line: the goddess who called the Pylians out in the night (714–716) now ends the pursuit.

sentences.t: ἔνθ’ ἄνδρα κτείνας πύματον λίπον·
sentences.l: There, having killed a man, the last one, I left him;
sentences.i: There I killed one last man and left him;
sentences.n: ἔνθ’ ‘there’ is the place where the chase ended, named at 756–757. κτείνας is the aorist participle of κτείνω ‘kill’, and πύματον ‘last’ is the accusative of πύματος. λίπον is the aorist of λείπω ‘leave’, so ‘having killed a last man, I left him’. The unit ends at ·, and αὐτὰρ Ἀχαιοί begins the next sentence in the same line.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ἀχαιοὶ
ἂψ ἀπὸ Βουπρασίοιο Πύλονδ’ ἔχον ὠκέας ἵππους,
πάντες δ’ εὐχετόωντο θεῶν Διὶ Νέστορί τ’ ἀνδρῶν.
sentences.l:
but the Achaeans
back from Buprasium to Pylos held their swift horses,
and all prayed, of gods to Zeus, and of men to Nestor.
sentences.i: and the Achaeans drove their swift horses back from Buprasium to Pylos, and all of them offered their prayers, to Zeus among the gods and to Nestor among men.
sentences.n: The Achaeans here are the Pylians, Nestor’s own side. ἂψ ἀπὸ Βουπρασίοιο is ‘back from Buprasium’, with the epic genitive; Πύλονδ’ is ‘to Pylos’ with -δε; ἔχον ὠκέας ἵππους is ‘held their swift horses’, i.e. drove them. εὐχετόωντο is the open form of εὐχετάομαι, which can mean ‘pray’ and ‘vow’ or ‘boast’; here it covers the thanks and honour paid to Zeus (θεῶν Διί) and to Nestor (ἀνδρῶν Νέστορι).

sentences.t: ὣς ἔον, εἴ ποτ’ ἔον γε, μετ’ ἀνδράσιν.
sentences.l: So was I, if ever I was, among men.
sentences.i: That is what I was, if ever I was, among men.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔον, εἴ ποτ’ ἔον γε is ‘so I was, if ever I was’: ἔον is the epic first-person imperfect of εἰμί. The phrase closes the tale of the raid and sets Nestor’s past at a distance, in the voice of an old man. μετ’ ἀνδράσιν is ‘among men’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ἀχιλλεὺς
οἶος τῆς ἀρετῆς ἀπονήσεται·
sentences.l:
But Achilles
alone will have the benefit of his excellence;
sentences.i: But Achilles alone will have the benefit of his excellence;
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ Ἀχιλλεύς turns from the past to the present. οἶος is ‘alone’. ἀπονήσεται is the future middle of ἀπονίνημι ‘have profit or enjoyment of’, taking the genitive τῆς ἀρετῆς ‘his excellence’; ἀρετή is the Greek word for a man’s fighting quality, and τῆς points to it as his. The sentence is bitter: he alone will profit from it.

sentences.t:
ἦ τέ μιν οἴω
πολλὰ μετακλαύσεσθαι ἐπεί κ’ ἀπὸ λαὸς ὄληται.
sentences.l:
and I suspect that he
will greatly weep afterwards, when the people have perished.
sentences.i: and I suspect he will weep greatly afterwards, when the troops have perished.
sentences.n: ἦ τέ μιν οἴω ‘and I suspect him’ governs an infinitive: οἴω (ὀΐω) ‘I suspect’ takes μιν … μετακλαύσεσθαι ‘that he will weep afterwards’, with the future infinitive of μετακλαίω and πολλά used adverbially, ‘much’. ἐπεί κ’ … ὄληται is ‘when … has perished’, the aorist subjunctive of ἀπόλλυμι with tmesis (ἀπὸ … ὄληται); λαός is the army, a singular noun with a singular verb.

sentences.t:
ὦ πέπον ἦ μὲν σοί γε Μενοίτιος ὧδ’ ἐπέτελλεν
ἤματι τῷ ὅτε σ’ ἐκ Φθίης Ἀγαμέμνονι πέμπε,
sentences.l:
O good one, truly to you Menoetius thus laid his charge
on that day when from Phthia to Agamemnon he sent you,
sentences.i: My good fellow, truly Menoetius gave you his charge in this way on the day when he sent you from Phthia to Agamemnon,
sentences.n: Nestor now turns from his own tale to Patroclus’ own past. ὦ πέπον ‘O good one’ opens the same address at 9.252; the second line here is 9.253 word for word, and its English is the same. ἦ μέν is ‘truly’, σοί γε ‘to you’; ἐπέτελλεν is the imperfect of ἐπιτέλλω ‘lay a charge on’, ὧδε ‘thus’. Menoetius is Patroclus’ father, and πέμπε is the imperfect of πέμπω ‘send’.

sentences.t:
νῶϊ δέ τ’ ἔνδον ἐόντες ἐγὼ καὶ δῖος Ὀδυσσεὺς
πάντα μάλ’ ἐν μεγάροις ἠκούομεν ὡς ἐπέτελλε.
sentences.l:
and we two, being within, I and heavenly Odysseus,
in the halls heard everything well, how he laid his charge.
sentences.i: and we two, I and heavenly Odysseus, being inside in the halls, heard it all well, how he gave his charge.
sentences.n: νῶϊ ‘we two’ is a dual, and the apposition ἐγὼ καὶ δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς names the pair; δῖος ‘heavenly’ is the stock epithet. ἔνδον ἐόντες ‘being within’ and ἐν μεγάροις ‘in the halls’ give the place, the halls of Peleus’ house in the next lines. ἠκούομεν is the imperfect ‘we were hearing’, with πάντα μάλ’ ‘everything well’, and ὡς ἐπέτελλε ‘how he laid his charge’ takes up the verb of 765.

sentences.t:
Πηλῆος δ’ ἱκόμεσθα δόμους εὖ ναιετάοντας
λαὸν ἀγείροντες κατ’ Ἀχαιΐδα πουλυβότειραν.
sentences.l:
And the house of Peleus we came to, well-inhabited,
gathering the people throughout Achaea, the much-nourishing.
sentences.i: And we came to the well-inhabited house of Peleus, as we gathered the troops throughout Achaea, that feeds so many.
sentences.n: Πηλῆος δόμους εὖ ναιετάοντας is ‘the well-inhabited house of Peleus’, εὖ ναιετάοντας being the stock phrase for a household full of people. ἱκόμεσθα is ‘we came’, with the ending -μεσθα. λαὸν ἀγείροντες is ‘gathering the people’, and κατ’ Ἀχαιΐδα πουλυβότειραν is ‘throughout Achaea’, Ἀχαιΐς being the Achaean land, with the epithet ‘much-nourishing’ (‘that feeds so many’).

sentences.t:
ἔνθα δ’ ἔπειθ’ ἥρωα Μενοίτιον εὕρομεν ἔνδον
ἠδὲ σέ, πὰρ δ’ Ἀχιλῆα·
sentences.l:
And there then the hero Menoetius we found within,
and you, and beside you Achilles;
sentences.i: And there we found the hero Menoetius inside, and you, and Achilles beside you;
sentences.n: ἔνθα δ’ ἔπειτα ‘and there then’ begins the scene at Peleus’ house. ἥρωα Μενοίτιον is ‘the hero Menoetius’, ἥρως being Homer’s word for a warrior of the old days. εὕρομεν ἔνδον is ‘we found within’; ἠδὲ σέ ‘and you’ is Patroclus, and πὰρ δ’ Ἀχιλῆα is ‘and beside (you) Achilles’, πάρ being παρά with the vowel lost.

sentences.t:
γέρων δ’ ἱππηλάτα Πηλεὺς
πίονα μηρία καῖε βοὸς Διὶ τερπικεραύνῳ
αὐλῆς ἐν χόρτῳ· ἔχε δὲ χρύσειον ἄλεισον
σπένδων αἴθοπα οἶνον ἐπ’ αἰθομένοις ἱεροῖσι.
sentences.l:
and the old man, horse-driver Peleus,
was burning fat thigh-pieces of an ox for Zeus delighting-in-the-thunderbolt
in the enclosure of the court; and he held a golden goblet,
pouring the fire-faced wine over the burning sacrifices.
sentences.i: and Peleus, the old horse-driver, was burning the fat thigh-pieces of an ox for Zeus, who delights in the thunderbolt, in the enclosure of the courtyard; and he held a golden goblet, pouring wine that has the look of fire over the burning sacrifices.
sentences.n: A sacrifice is under way. γέρων ἱππηλάτα Πηλεύς, ‘Peleus, the old horse-driver’, has the formula that the Odyssey uses of Nestor. πίονα μηρία are the ‘fat thigh-pieces’ burned for the god; Διὶ τερπικεραύνῳ is ‘to Zeus delighting-in-the-thunderbolt’, from τέρπω ‘delight’ and κεραυνός. αὐλῆς ἐν χόρτῳ is ‘in the enclosure of the court’. He holds a golden ἄλεισον ‘goblet’, σπένδων ‘pouring’ αἴθοπα οἶνον, ‘wine with the look of fire’, ἐπ’ αἰθομένοις ἱεροῖσι ‘over the burning sacrifices’.

sentences.t:
σφῶϊ μὲν ἀμφὶ βοὸς ἕπετον κρέα, νῶϊ δ’ ἔπειτα
στῆμεν ἐνὶ προθύροισι·
sentences.l:
You two were busy about the flesh of the ox, and we two then
stood in the forecourt;
sentences.i: You two were busy with the flesh of the ox, and we two then stood in the forecourt;
sentences.n: σφῶϊ ‘you two’ (Patroclus and Achilles) and νῶϊ ‘we two’ (Nestor and Odysseus) are duals. ἕπετον is the dual imperfect of ἕπω ‘be busy about’, with ἀμφὶ … κρέα ‘about the flesh’ of the ox; στῆμεν is ἔστημεν ‘we stood’. ἐνὶ προθύροισι is ‘in the forecourt’, πρόθυρον being the space before the door. The unit ends at ·, in mid-line.

sentences.t:
ταφὼν δ’ ἀνόρουσεν Ἀχιλλεύς,
ἐς δ’ ἄγε χειρὸς ἑλών, κατὰ δ’ ἑδριάασθαι ἄνωγε,
ξείνιά τ’ εὖ παρέθηκεν, ἅ τε ξείνοις θέμις ἐστίν.
sentences.l:
and amazed sprang up Achilles,
and led us in, taking us by the hand, and to sit down he bade us,
and set out well the things due to guests, as is the custom for guests.
sentences.i: Achilles sprang up in amazement, and took us by the hand and led us in, and bade us sit down, and set out the hospitality due to guests, as is the custom for guests.
sentences.n: ταφών ‘amazed’ is the aorist participle of the verb that goes with τέθηπα ‘be astounded’; ἀνόρουσεν is ‘sprang up’. The middle line is the line used of Nestor’s reception of Patroclus at 646; here the object of ἐς … ἄγε (tmesis, ‘led in’) is left unspoken, and the English says ‘us’, Nestor and Odysseus. ξείνιά τ’ εὖ παρέθηκεν is ‘set out well the things due to guests’, and ἅ τε ξείνοις θέμις ἐστίν ‘as is the custom for guests’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ τάρπημεν ἐδητύος ἠδὲ ποτῆτος,
ἦρχον ἐγὼ μύθοιο κελεύων ὔμμ’ ἅμ’ ἕπεσθαι·
sentences.l:
But when we had taken our fill of food and of drink,
I began the speech, urging you two to follow with us;
sentences.i: When we had taken our fill of food and drink, I began to speak, urging you both to come with us;
sentences.n: τάρπημεν is the passive aorist of τέρπω used as ‘were satisfied’, with the genitives ἐδητύος ‘of food’ and ποτῆτος ‘of drink’; the clause is an old formula for the end of a meal. ἦρχον ἐγὼ μύθοιο is ‘I began the speech’, ἄρχω taking the genitive. ὔμμ’ is the epic ‘you’, here two persons, with κελεύων ‘urging’ and the infinitive ἕπεσθαι ‘to follow’, ἅμ’ ‘along with (us)’.

sentences.t: σφὼ δὲ μάλ’ ἠθέλετον, τὼ δ’ ἄμφω πόλλ’ ἐπέτελλον.
sentences.l: and you two were very willing, and they both gave many commands.
sentences.i: and you two were most willing, and the two old men both charged you strictly.
sentences.n: σφώ is the nominative dual ‘you two’, and ἠθέλετον is the dual imperfect of ἐθέλω ‘be willing’, with the long-vowel augment ἠ-. τὼ δ’ ἄμφω is ‘and those two, both’: τώ is a dual pronoun for the two fathers, Peleus and Menoetius, whose charges follow. πόλλ’ ἐπέτελλον is ‘gave many commands’.

sentences.t:
Πηλεὺς μὲν ᾧ παιδὶ γέρων ἐπέτελλ’ Ἀχιλῆϊ
αἰὲν ἀριστεύειν καὶ ὑπείροχον ἔμμεναι ἄλλων·
sentences.l:
Peleus, the old man, to his own son Achilles laid his charge
always to be the best and to be one standing above others;
sentences.i: Peleus, the old man, gave his son Achilles his charge, always to be the best and to stand above the others;
sentences.n: The two charges are given in turn, Peleus’ first. ᾧ is the possessive ‘his own’, and Ἀχιλῆϊ is the Homeric dative of Ἀχιλλεύς. The charge is told in infinitives, not quoted. αἰὲν ἀριστεύειν καὶ ὑπείροχον ἔμμεναι ἄλλων is ‘always to be the best and to be one standing above others’, the same words as the charge Glaucus’ father gave him at 6.208, with the same English.

sentences.t: σοὶ δ’ αὖθ’ ὧδ’ ἐπέτελλε Μενοίτιος Ἄκτορος υἱός·
sentences.l: and to you in turn thus laid his charge Menoetius, Actor’s son:
sentences.i: and to you Menoetius, Actor’s son, gave this charge in turn:
sentences.n: σοὶ δ’ αὖθ’ ὧδ’ ἐπέτελλε is ‘and to you, in turn, he laid his charge thus’, αὖθ’ being αὖτε ‘in turn’. Μενοίτιος Ἄκτορος υἱός is ‘Menoetius, Actor’s son’. His words follow in direct speech inside Nestor’s, up to 789; the English marks them with single quotation marks.

sentences.t:
τέκνον ἐμὸν γενεῇ μὲν ὑπέρτερός ἐστιν Ἀχιλλεύς,
πρεσβύτερος δὲ σύ ἐσσι· βίῃ δ’ ὅ γε πολλὸν ἀμείνων.
sentences.l:
‘My child, in birth Achilles is higher,
but older are you; and in might he is much the better;
sentences.i: ‘My child, Achilles is higher than you in birth, but you are the older; and in might he is much the better;
sentences.n: τέκνον ἐμόν is ‘my child’. γενεῇ μὲν ὑπέρτερος is ‘higher in birth’, γενεῇ being a dative of respect. πρεσβύτερος ‘older’ is a comparative, and ἐσσι is the epic second singular of εἰμί. βίῃ δ’ ὅ γε πολλὸν ἀμείνων is ‘in might he is much the better’: βίη is ‘might’, ἀμείνων the comparative of ἀγαθός, and πολλόν an adverb. The unit stops at the full stop printed after ἀμείνων.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ εὖ οἱ φάσθαι πυκινὸν ἔπος ἠδ’ ὑποθέσθαι
καί οἱ σημαίνειν· ὃ δὲ πείσεται εἰς ἀγαθόν περ.
sentences.l:
but speak to him well a shrewd word, and give him counsel,
and direct him; and he will obey, to his good indeed.’
sentences.i: but speak to him well, with a shrewd word, and counsel him, and guide him; and he will obey, to his good.’
sentences.n: φάσθαι ‘speak’, ὑποθέσθαι ‘give counsel’ and σημαίνειν ‘direct, give signs’ are infinitives used for commands, with οἱ ‘to him’ (Achilles). εὖ goes with φάσθαι, and πυκινὸν ἔπος is ‘a shrewd word’. ὃ δὲ πείσεται εἰς ἀγαθόν περ is ‘and he will obey, to his good’: πείσεται is the future of πείθομαι ‘obey’, and εἰς ἀγαθόν περ ‘to his good indeed’. The quoted words end here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἐπέτελλ’ ὃ γέρων, σὺ δὲ λήθεαι·
sentences.l: So he laid his charge, the old man, but you forget;
sentences.i: So the old man gave his charge, and you forget it;
sentences.n: ὣς ἐπέτελλ’ ὃ γέρων closes the quotation, and is word for word 9.259, with that line’s English: ὃ γέρων ‘the old man’ is now Menoetius. λήθεαι is the epic second singular of the middle of λήθομαι ‘forget’ (the uncontracted -εαι, Attic -ῃ), and the present means that Patroclus is forgetting the charge now.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἔτι καὶ νῦν
ταῦτ’ εἴποις Ἀχιλῆϊ δαΐφρονι αἴ κε πίθηται.
sentences.l:
but even now still
you might say this to wise-minded Achilles, if he may be persuaded.
sentences.i: But even now you might still say this to wise-hearted Achilles, in case he can be persuaded.
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἔτι καὶ νῦν is ‘but even now still’. ταῦτ’ εἴποις is the optative of polite suggestion, ‘you might say this’. δαΐφρονι is an epithet of disputed meaning, ‘wise’ or ‘fierce’ in mind; the translation takes ‘wise-minded’ in l and ‘wise-hearted’ in i, as it does wherever the word stands. αἴ κε πίθηται is ‘if perhaps he may be persuaded’, the aorist subjunctive middle of πείθω.

sentences.t:
τίς δ’ οἶδ’ εἴ κέν οἱ σὺν δαίμονι θυμὸν ὀρίναις
παρειπών;
sentences.l:
And who knows whether with some power you might stir his heart,
talking him round?
sentences.i: And who knows whether, with some power’s help, you might stir his heart by talking him round?
sentences.n: τίς δ’ οἶδ’ εἴ κέν … is ‘and who knows whether … might’, a question that implies the answer may be yes. σὺν δαίμονι is ‘with some power’: δαίμων is an unnamed divine power at work, here helping Patroclus. θυμὸν ὀρίναις is ‘you might stir his heart’, ὀρίναις being the optative of ὀρίνω. παρειπών is the aorist participle of παρεῖπον ‘talk over, persuade’. The unit ends at the Greek question mark.

sentences.t: ἀγαθὴ δὲ παραίφασίς ἐστιν ἑταίρου.
sentences.l: good is the persuasion of a companion.
sentences.i: a companion’s persuasion is a good thing.
sentences.n: ἀγαθή ‘good’ stands first and παραίφασις ‘persuasion’ is a rare noun, from παραφημί ‘talk round, encourage’, for persuading by speaking beside someone. ἑταίρου is the genitive of ἑταῖρος ‘companion’. The line is a general statement, so ἐστίν is in the present.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ τινα φρεσὶν ᾗσι θεοπροπίην ἀλεείνει
καί τινά οἱ πὰρ Ζηνὸς ἐπέφραδε πότνια μήτηρ,
sentences.l:
But if in his own mind some prophecy he is shunning,
and some one from Zeus his lady mother has pointed out to him,
sentences.i: But if he is shunning some prophecy in his own mind, and his lady mother has told him of one from Zeus,
sentences.n: Nestor gives two reasons why Achilles may be holding back. εἰ δέ … ἀλεείνει is ‘but if he is shunning’, ἀλεείνω meaning ‘avoid’, with θεοπροπίην ‘a prophecy’. φρεσὶν ᾗσι is ‘in his own mind’, ᾗσι being the possessive. In καί τινά … ἐπέφραδε the object τινά is again ‘some prophecy’, understood from the first clause, with πὰρ Ζηνός ‘from Zeus’; ἐπέφραδε is the aorist of φράζω ‘point out, tell’. πότνια μήτηρ ‘lady mother’ is Achilles’ mother.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ σέ περ προέτω, ἅμα δ’ ἄλλος λαὸς ἑπέσθω
Μυρμιδόνων, αἴ κέν τι φόως Δαναοῖσι γένηαι·
sentences.l:
yet you at least let him send forth, and along with you let the other people
of the Myrmidons follow, if somehow a light you may become to the Danaans;
sentences.i: at least let him send you out, and let the rest of the Myrmidon troops follow with you, in the hope that you may somehow become a light to the Danaans;
sentences.n: ἀλλά … περ is ‘yet … at least’: if Achilles himself will not fight, he may let Patroclus. προέτω is the aorist imperative of προίημι ‘send forth’, with Achilles understood as subject, and ἑπέσθω is the aorist imperative of ἕπομαι ‘follow’. ἄλλος λαὸς Μυρμιδόνων is ‘the rest of the people of the Myrmidons’. αἴ κέν τι φόως Δαναοῖσι γένηαι is ‘if somehow you may become a light to the Danaans’, as at 8.282: φόως is φῶς ‘light’ as a figure of rescue, and γένηαι the epic second singular subjunctive.

sentences.t:
καί τοι τεύχεα καλὰ δότω πόλεμον δὲ φέρεσθαι,
αἴ κέ σε τῷ εἴσκοντες ἀπόσχωνται πολέμοιο
Τρῶες,
sentences.l:
and let him give you his fine armour to carry into the war,
in case, taking you for him, they may hold off from the war,
the Trojans,
sentences.i: and let him give you his fine armour to carry into the war, in case the Trojans, taking you for him, hold back from war,
sentences.n: καί τοι τεύχεα καλὰ δότω is ‘and let him give you his fine armour’: δότω is the aorist imperative of δίδωμι, and τοι is the dative ‘to you’. πόλεμον δὲ φέρεσθαι is ‘to carry into the war’, with -δε of direction. αἴ κέ σε τῷ εἴσκοντες is ‘in case, taking you for him’, εἴσκοντες being the participle of εἴσκω ‘liken, take to be’. ἀπόσχωνται πολέμοιο is ‘hold themselves back from the war’; the subject Τρῶες is held to the next line, so the unit ends at the comma.

sentences.t:
ἀναπνεύσωσι δ’ ἀρήϊοι υἷες Ἀχαιῶν
τειρόμενοι·
sentences.l:
and the warlike sons of the Achaeans may get breath again,
worn down;
sentences.i: and the warlike sons of the Achaeans, worn down, get their breath back;
sentences.n: ἀναπνεύσωσι is the aorist subjunctive of ἀναπνέω ‘get breath again’, continuing the αἴ κε clause. The subject is ἀρήϊοι υἷες Ἀχαιῶν ‘the warlike sons of the Achaeans’, ἀρήϊος being the adjective from Ἄρης, and τειρόμενοι ‘worn down’ is the passive participle of τείρω.

sentences.t: ὀλίγη δέ τ’ ἀνάπνευσις πολέμοιο.
sentences.l: and small is the breathing-space from war.
sentences.i: and the breathing-space from war is small.
sentences.n: ὀλίγη δέ τ’ ἀνάπνευσις πολέμοιο is a general remark, with the epic τε marking what is always true: ‘small is the breathing-space from war’. ἀνάπνευσις is the noun that goes with the verb ἀναπνέω of the line before. The Greek does not say whether the shortness is a reason for haste or a reassurance that a little is enough; the next line says what even a little allows.

sentences.t:
ῥεῖα δέ κ’ ἀκμῆτες κεκμηότας ἄνδρας ἀϋτῇ
ὤσαισθε προτὶ ἄστυ νεῶν ἄπο καὶ κλισιάων.
sentences.l:
And easily you, fresh, men who are weary, with a battle-cry,
could push back to the town, away from the ships and the huts.”
sentences.i: And easily, being fresh, you could drive men who are tired out, with a battle-cry, back to the town, away from the ships and the huts.”
sentences.n: ῥεῖα δέ κ’ … ὤσαισθε is ‘and easily you could push’: ὤσαισθε is the aorist optative middle of ὠθέω, second plural, with κε, addressed to Patroclus and the Myrmidons. ἀκμῆτες ‘fresh’ is set against κεκμηότας ‘wearied’, the perfect participle of κάμνω; ἄνδρας is the Trojans. ἀϋτῇ is ‘with a battle-cry’. νεῶν ἄπο … κλισιάων is ‘away from the ships and the huts’, with ἄπο after its noun. Nestor’s speech ends here.
